query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) under tribocorrosion, the overall degradation is governed by the formation and stability of an in-situ, wear‐induced passive oxide/composite layer (e.g. a dense ZrTiO4 or similar protective compound) that mediates the balance between mechanical removal (wear) and corrosion resistance. When a thermal or compositional treatment promotes the formation of such a stable passivating film on the surface, it both limits corrosion damage and retards wear-induced degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A as-deposited or as-cast high-entropy alloy (such as an amorphous or nanocrystalline AlCrTiZrMo-based film) with a reactive surface but without a well-developed protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal treatment (thermal shock/annealing in air) or dopant (e.g. B addition) that promotes the in-situ formation of a dense, adherent composite oxide film on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Tribological sliding tests conducted in a corrosive environment (e.g. 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) under identical mechanical loading, with one set of specimens pre-treated to form the passive layer and a matched baseline set left untreated.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent oxide/composite film (e.g. ZrTiO4 or similar) that resists mechanical spallation and acts as a barrier to corrosive agents.
generation.mechanism: Wear removes surface material while also continuously exposing fresh metal that rapidly forms a passive oxide. A pre-formed, stable passive film reduces the rate of corrosion by limiting ion transport and oxidation. The interplay between mechanical removal (wear) and re-passivation (corrosion) determines the net degradation. Thus, enhancing film formation shifts the balance toward lower corrosion contribution even when mechanical wear occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-treated HEA will exhibit a lower total mass loss in tribocorrosion tests due primarily to a reduced corrosion component, while the wear contribution may remain similar. In other words, overall degradation is significantly reduced relative to the untreated baseline, with measured corrosion current densities and potential shifts indicating improved passivation.
generation.baseline: An identical HEA specimen without thermal or compositional treatment (i.e. without the induced protective oxide layer).
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold under moderate to high contact pressures that allow sufficient passive film regeneration, but may fail in conditions with excessive mechanical removal (e.g. extreme loads or abrasive environments) or in alloy systems that lack the necessary oxide-forming elements.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between the rates of wear-induced oxide removal and the reformation of the passivating film is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition, oxide chemistry, and specific test parameters. The threshold of mechanical stress where the protective effect fails is also not precisely defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA specimens with identical composition and microstructure. Group A is subjected to a thermal treatment known to promote passive layer formation, while Group B remains as-prepared. Use a tribometer setup in a corrosive medium (e.g. 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) to perform coupled wear-corrosion tests under controlled, identical load and sliding velocity conditions. Monitor the evolution of the surface with in-situ electrochemical noise analysis and post-test mass loss measurements.
measurements: Total mass loss after a defined wear-corrosion cycle
Electrochemical parameters (e.g. corrosion current density, open-circuit potential) during testing
Surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide layer continuity and thickness
Wear track morphology and depth analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated group (Group A) does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the corrosion component (e.g. lower corrosion current density and more positive OCP) and overall mass loss relative to the untreated baseline (Group B) under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that the passive oxide layer governs the coupled tribocorrosion response is falsified.

Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film

Abstract: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution

Abstract: AbstractThe challenge of cavitation erosion (CE) in flow-handling components of marine engineering has promoted the development of advanced materials due to safety incidents and economic costs. High entropy alloys (HEAs), known for high hardness and corrosion resistance, emerge as promising candidates. This paper delved into the CE characteristics of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA when subjected to the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, elucidating the synergistic effect of CE-corrosion. The quantitative analysis revealed that CE-corrosion synergy contributed 48.02% to total CE mass loss, primarily attributed to corrosion-induced CE damage. Meanwhile, electrochemical noise (EN) was utilized to reveal the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution combined with the morphologies observation and surface roughness. Extended CE time compromised the corrosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA and diminished the impact of selective phase corrosion on the surface. Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding

Abstract: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase.
